results.title: Sample size calculations in human electrophysiology (EEG and ERP) studies: A systematic review and recommendations for increased rigor - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Sample size calculations in human electrophysiology (EEG and ERP) studies: A systematic review and recommendations for increased rigor. We systematically reviewed 100 randomly selected clinical human electrophysiology studies from six high impact journals that frequently publish electroencephalography (EEG) and event-related potential (ERP) research to determine the proportion of studies that reported sample size calculations, as well as the proportion of studies reporting the necessary components to complete such calculations. Increased focus on sample size calculations, utilization of registered reports, and presenting information detailing sample size calculations and statistics for future researchers are needed and will increase sample size-related scientific rigor in human electrophysiology research. An additional recommendation that may strengthen research is to complete *a priori* sample size calculations to ensure that studies are sufficiently powered, to reduce the probability of false negative findings, and to ensure that effect sizes are not inflated (Button et al., 2013, Ioannidis, 2005, Ioannidis, 2008, Sawyer and Ball, 1981, Sterne and Smith, 2001). Furthermore, the lack of information in the literature, such as effect sizes or variance components, that is needed to perform power analyses may make it difficult to conduct sample size calculations to ensure an appropriate sample size is collected (Guo et al., 2014). Sample size calculations, such as a power analysis, estimating the number of participants to obtain a desired confidence interval width, or utilizing Bayesian estimators (Lenth, 2001, Wang et al., 2005) inform reviewers and readers if the reported sample size is adequate enough to accurately detect the effects of interest and determine if the effects may be inflated (see Button et al., 2013, Ioannidis, 2005). In fact, our own lab and research is subject to this critique; however, no studies that we are aware of have systematically examined human electrophysiology (including EEG and ERPs) studies to report if quantitative sample size comparisons are being utilized or the effect sizes and variance components needed to conduct sample size calculation are being reported. * ### Methodological reporting behavior, sample sizes, and statistical power in studies of event-related potentials: Barriers to reproducibility and replicability.

results.title: What is a good sample size for a study?
results.content: # What is a good sample size for a study? In this article, we will delve into the nitty-gritty of how to determine a good sample size for your study. But, with the power comes the responsibility to ensure accurate representation of the population we’re trying to understand by selecting a representative sample When determining a sample size, several factors require consideration: • **Studied population size:** The larger the population from which you’re selecting subjects, the larger your required sample size. • **Desired level of statistical precision:** The more granular your results need to be, the larger the sample size required. • **Expected effect size of the study:** If small changes are expected, **a larger sample size provides more power to detect true effects**. • **Type of study design (e.g., survey or experiment):** Different experimental designs require different sample size calculations. • **Researchers’ goals and resources** (time, budget) To calculate sample sizes, researchers often rely on **Cochran’s Formula**. This approximation formula helps determine the *minimum* sample size requirements for a study: formula: n = (za^2 \* np(1-p)) + (Zb^2 \* (1–p)) Z = Z-score ( depends on the desired level of confidence) a = tolerance level (acceptable margin error) p = population prevalence (proportion of affected individuals) b = binomial proportion (desired ratio of positive to negative data) **Sample size as a function of desired statistically significant effect size** Understanding the concept of **\*\**effect size* will help you determine a *good* sample size!** Effect size\* *measure the magnitude of the proposed relationship between variables. **Best-practice tips for selecting a robust sample size** • Establish clear research objectives and assumptions • Consult with literature and experts in the subject area • Perform data-driven sample size calculations **(e.g., nQuery software)** • Consider using **pockets of power** (heterogeneous subgroups can increase precision) • Implement **stratified sample selection** to minimize unwanted biases • Regularly review and adjust sample sizes as needed **Lessons learned and takeaways for researchers** • **Sample size alone is not the sole concern**; consider factors ranging from population size to ethereal constraints. • Reliable sample size calculations can shield against errors and provide powerful insights. Determine a good sample size for your study by ensuring you have a comprehensive picture of the factors influencing yours.
